title: Hobbycast Episode 7 - Ten Great Science Fiction Novels
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vUEmbLAxZ0Y

A science-fiction month on the channel spills into the podcast, and Daniel (@dungeondive) reads out ten novels from a physical stack, in stack order, with the back-cover copy quoted from the actual editions on his lap. Explicitly not a top ten and not a list of books you must read — just ten he loves.

Rudy Rucker's *White Light* (1980) opens as "math punk," a transrealist comedy about proving a number greater than infinity. Olaf Stapledon's *Sirius* (1944) is the oldest and the saddest — a dog with a human mind, and the only book to make him cry in public. Alan Lightman's *Einstein's Dreams* (1992), each chapter a dream about time. Bradbury's *The Martian Chronicles* (1950), darker on every reread than he remembers. Sturgeon's *To Marry Medusa* (1958), read in one sitting on a two-hour bus ride. Philip Palmer's *Version 43* (2010), the fun one — gonzo, ultraviolent, underrated. Russo's Carlucci trilogy for noir cyberpunk. Simak's *Way Station* (1963), pastoral SF he owns in seven editions.

Two get the strongest claims: Bester's *The Stars My Destination* as the best SF novel ever written, and *Martian Time-Slip* as the best Philip K. Dick — blue-collar protagonists on Mars, madness as subject.

----

Which of these ten would you hand to someone who says they don't read science fiction?
